questions.q: What does `kubectl get hpa` reveal about the storefront app?
options: The HPA is crashing and not functioning
minReplicas is set to 10 with CPU utilization at only 22%, far below the 70% scale-up target
The app has no autoscaler configured at all
maxReplicas is set lower than minReplicas
questions.explain: The HPA is working exactly as configured; the configured floor of 10 replicas is the actual problem, not a malfunction.

questions.q: What does pulling p95 CPU utilization over two weeks confirm?
options: That ten replicas are barely enough to handle peak traffic
That utilization is low and flat, and two replicas would comfortably cover real traffic with headroom
That the app needs even more replicas than ten
That utilization data isn't available for this workload
questions.explain: Real p95 utilization data, not a guess, confirms two replicas is the right baseline — the same right-sizing discipline applied to autoscaling.

questions.q: Where did the minReplicas: 10 setting actually come from?
options: A random default value in the Helm chart

Terraform's Lesson 4 module referenced the 'peak-season' scaling profile (minReplicas 10/maxReplicas 20) instead of the 'standard' profile (2/6), most likely copied from a different, higher-traffic environment's config
Someone manually edited the HPA in the Kubernetes dashboard
A bug in the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler controller itself
questions.explain: The root cause is a Terraform module referencing the wrong named scaling profile, not a Kubernetes bug or manual edit.

questions.q: Why does running 10 replicas instead of 2 cost real money beyond just the extra pods?
options: Extra pods have no cost impact at all
The cluster autoscaler keeps roughly 3 extra nodes running continuously to host the idle extra pods, plus associated load balancer and disk overhead
AKS charges per HTTP request regardless of replica count
Only the Terraform state file grows larger
questions.explain: Extra always-on pods force the cluster autoscaler to keep extra nodes alive to host them, which is where most of the real cost overshoot comes from.

questions.q: What are the correct 'standard' profile values that should have been used for Driftwood's everyday production traffic?
options: minReplicas: 10, maxReplicas: 20
minReplicas: 0, maxReplicas: 2
minReplicas: 2, maxReplicas: 6
minReplicas: 2, maxReplicas: 2
questions.explain: The 'standard' profile (2/6) matches Driftwood's real observed traffic, keeping a generous ceiling for genuine spikes while fixing the floor.
